reports.name: Junior Caminero
reports.published_report: Forty-six home runs projected at age 23 is the headline, and the Statcast profile backs the number up. His average exit velocity sits at 93.0 mph with a 50.7% hard-hit rate, and the .515 xSLG suggests the raw power translates cleanly to what shows up in the box score. The 12.4% walk rate is what separates him from a pure masher — it's how a .363 OBP ends up next to that slug, and it's why the projection lands at .911 OPS across 701 plate appearances. Everything here hinges on the contact holding; the whiff rate and chase rate both sit near the middle of the league, so if pitchers find a reliable way to exploit the zone he can't cover, the walks shrink before the power does.

reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The tension in the profile is that he's simultaneously one of the hardest hitters to make solid contact against and one of the more dangerous bats in the league once he connects. A 27.3% strikeout rate is the genuine liability here, fueled by a 34.0% chase rate that sits well below average in discipline terms, yet a 12.0% walk rate somehow survives the aggression, and when he does make contact, 48.7% of it is hard-hit with a 12.3% barrel rate that explains why xSLG sits at .469 and xwOBA at .361. The projection fills in the picture: 34 home runs and 39 stolen bases across 714 plate appearances, a .520 SLG that assumes the exit-velo quality keeps outrunning the swing-and-miss, and that's the hinge, because if pitchers ever fully exploit the chase numbers and the strikeout rate climbs further, the counting stats compress fast. Right now the batted-ball profile is loud enough to carry the contact problem, and at 29.5 ft/s sprint speed he has the legs to compound every mistake a pitcher makes.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .408 xwOBA and a 2.72 xERA on the same card — that's the whole argument, and there's no softening it. On the hitting side, the contact quality is elite across every shape: 93.4 mph average exit velocity, a 16.7% barrel rate, an xSLG of .576, all sitting at the 95th percentile or better, and a 13.5% walk rate that turns a 23.0% strikeout rate into a manageable trade-off. The pitching profile is just as clean, with a 30.4% whiff rate and a barrel rate against of only 3.8% explaining why the xERA lands where it does. The one real dependency is innings: if the elbow holds and he takes the mound regularly, this is a historically rare profile doing exactly what it looks like; if the pitching side stalls, you still have a .939 OPS projection across 693 plate appearances and a hitter who belongs in the conversation with anyone in the sport.

reports.name: James Wood
reports.published_report: The contact-and-power profile here is as loud as it gets: a 20.8% barrel rate and a 95.1 mph average exit velocity both sitting at the 100th percentile, with an xSLG of .585 that says the projection's .523 SLG is conservative. Wood also runs a 16.8% walk rate that almost no hitter at this level can match. The whole thing hinges on whether a 28.6% strikeout rate, bottom 12% of the league, ever comes down, because at the current whiff rate the gap between what he should hit and what he actually hits stays wide. If it does compress even modestly, you're talking about a legitimate MVP-caliber season out of a 23-year-old; if it doesn't, the .387 OBP and the power still make him a middle-of-the-order force, just a noisier one.

reports.name: CJ Abrams
reports.published_report: The power-speed combination here is legitimate, but the profile hinges almost entirely on whether Statcast is measuring a better hitter than his chase rate suggests. His xwOBA sits at .345 and his xSLG at .454, numbers that reflect real contact quality when he does connect, yet a 37.3% chase rate in the 12th percentile means pitchers have a reliable plan against him, and the 29.5% whiff rate compounds the exposure. The projection absorbs some of that risk, landing at .276/.348/.517 with 36 home runs and 30 steals across 681 plate appearances, which is a genuinely useful fantasy asset at shortstop if the contact holds. If the chase rate doesn't improve, the strikeouts pile up and the average drifts south of what the expected metrics promise, leaving a power-speed player with a leaky zone who is always one aggressive pitching staff from a frustrating month.

What works against him is a 35.2% chase rate and 30.9% whiff rate, both sitting near the bottom of the league, and a 7.8% walk rate that doesn't compensate for the exposure to spin away. reports.name: Jackson Merrill
reports.published_report: The contact quality shows up in the batted-ball shape, and the speed does too, but the plate discipline is what keeps this profile from being more than it is. Merrill's xSLG sits at .470 with a 47.4% hard-hit rate, yet a 36.6% chase rate drags his actual production back toward the mean, which is exactly why the projection lands at .249/.298/.428 rather than anything that resembles his underlying power shape. At 29.0 ft/s sprint speed he's a genuine stolen-base threat, and 27 projected steals on top of 25 home runs gives him a counting-stat floor that most outfielders his age can't match. The whole profile hinges on whether he ever tightens up the zone: if he does, the .470 xSLG starts translating; if he doesn't, he's a high-variance everyday player whose tools outpace his on-base ability by a significant margin.

reports.name: Jacob Wilson
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a puzzle with one beautiful piece and almost nothing else. Wilson's 11.4% strikeout rate sits in the 96th percentile, and the 14.8% whiff rate confirms the bat-to-ball is genuine. The problem is he chases 42.5% of pitches outside the zone, walks at just 3.6%, and makes exceptionally soft contact at 84.1 mph average exit velocity, which produces an xSLG of .348 and an xwOBA of .283. The projection's .275 AVG is achievable for a man who puts the ball in play this reliably, but the .713 OPS ceiling depends entirely on pitchers never learning to exploit that 42.5% chase rate with breaking balls off the plate, because when they do, he'll swing and he won't hit them hard enough to matter. A low-end regular at shortstop if the bat-to-ball keeps him on the field; a light-hitting bench piece the moment the league solves him.

reports.name: Lawrence Butler
reports.published_report: The chase rate is the most honest thing about his profile. The problem is what happens when pitchers do attack the zone: a 27.4% whiff rate drags his K% to 25.8%, and contact quality craters, with an xBA of .235 and an xSLG of .371 that look nothing like the hard-hit numbers suggest they should. He makes loud contact when he connects, 45.4% hard-hit, but the barrel rate sits at just 7.5%, which means a lot of that exit velocity is going somewhere other than the barrel. reports.name: Owen Murphy

reports.name: Shane McClanahan
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is a story about a pitcher still reassembling himself after Tommy John. His xERA sits at 4.12 and his strikeout rate at 22.2%, both hovering right around the league-average line, which is not where McClanahan lived before the surgery. What's still intact is the fastball, 95.6 mph, and enough movement to generate a 27.0% whiff rate and a 31.7% chase rate — the swing-and-miss shape is ahead of the results. The projection's 3.26 ERA over 137.1 innings is banking on that gap closing, on contact management tightening as he rebuilds command, because right now the barrel and hard-hit numbers suggest hitters who do make contact are doing damage. If the strikeout rate climbs back toward his pre-injury self, this is a mid-rotation anchor returning to form; if it doesn't, he's a back-end starter living on a fastball that still has life but not enough help around it.

reports.name: Jake Bauers
reports.published_report: The tension in the profile is that the contact tool and the power tool aren't playing the same sport. A 92.6 mph average exit velocity, 52.7% hard-hit rate, and 13.8% barrel rate are the calling card of a legitimate middle-of-the-order threat, but a 25.1% strikeout rate drags against all of it, and the xBA of .255 tells you exactly why: he squares it up when he swings, he just doesn't swing at enough good pitches to make consistent contact. The 20.5% chase rate is the saving grace, keeping the walk rate at 14.0% and propping the xwOBA to .366, which is why the projection carries .848 OPS across 559 PA despite the strikeout drag. If he keeps chasing at this rate and the hard contact holds, he's a legitimate everyday first baseman with 26-home-run upside; if the strikeout rate climbs and pitchers find the zone against him, the walk rate collapses with it and the whole profile deflates toward a platoon piece.

reports.published_report: Fifty stolen bases projected, two home runs. That's the entire offensive profile in a sentence, and the Statcast data explains exactly why: 84.9 mph average exit velocity and a 0.4% barrel rate both sit at the basement of the percentile chart, leaving a .272 xSLG that translates to a gap hitter with essentially no gap power. What saves the profile is discipline, a 10.8% walk rate and a 25.5% chase rate both meaningfully above average, which gets him to a .313 projected OBP out of a .229 batting average and keeps him useful in lineups that have nowhere else to hide him. The sprint speed at 29.7 ft/s is legitimate top-tier, the fielding percentile is 94th, and so the ceiling is an elite defensive middle infielder who runs into 50 steals and manufactures enough on-base to justify 522 plate appearances; the floor, if the contact quality never ticks up, is a defense-and-speed specialist whose .589 OPS becomes a liability the moment a team needs offense from that spot.

reports.name: Mason Montgomery

reports.name: Michael McGreevy
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is about as alarming as a pitcher's card gets: a 5.69 xERA, a .361 xwOBA allowed, and a 16.6% strikeout rate that sits near the bottom of qualified starters. Hitters are making hard contact at a 43.4% clip, and the 18.7% whiff rate explains why — there's simply not enough swing-and-miss to survive when command wobbles. The one saving grace is a 6.2% walk rate, which is genuinely good, and it's the only reason a 169.1-inning projection with a 3.81 ERA is even on the table: the whole read hinges on whether limiting free passes can keep balls in play from turning into crooked numbers at a 91.8 mph fastball velocity. If the contact suppression doesn't come around, what's left is a back-end starter logging innings for a contender without the stuff to protect leads.

reports.name: Alex Bregman
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile here is not a power hitter's card — a 4.6% barrel rate and 88.3 mph average exit velocity are well below average, but that undersells what Bregman actually is. He chases at 22.1% and whiffs at 15.9%, two of the better marks in the league, and an 11.0% walk rate that consistently turns at-bats into deep counts explains why the projection lands at a .345 OBP despite a .243 xBA. The bat-to-ball discipline is the engine; strip that out and the .756 OPS projection becomes hard to defend, but as long as the zone management holds, the contact skill papers over the soft exit velocity well enough to make him a solid everyday third baseman. The 90th-percentile fielding OAA is quiet context that a lot of people ignore.

If the raw power holds at the next level and the contact rate stabilizes, a left-handed swing that can punish right-handed pitching turns into a legitimate platoon piece; if the strikeout rate creeps and the walks stay thin, you're looking at a bench bat who earns his roster spot on pop alone.

reports.name: Mitch Jebb
reports.published_report: The contact is loud. Across AAA, AA, and A this season, Jebb is striking out in just 15% of plate appearances while posting a .290 average and a .374 OBP in 179 PA, and the translated strikeout rate of 19.6% compares favorably to the MLB mean of 22.0%, suggesting the bat-to-ball profile actually carries over. What it doesn't carry is power: an .161 ISO in the minors translates to .138 at the big-league level, and that gap between his OBP skills and his thump is the whole argument. Nine stolen bases add a wrinkle, but this profile lives or dies on whether the hit tool remains this clean against better stuff, because if the contact rate softens even modestly, there isn't enough pop to compensate, and organizational depth is the honest ceiling unless something changes in the power column.

reports.name: Manny Machado

reports.name: Brody Hopkins
reports.published_report: The strikeout stuff is loud — 106 punchouts across 85 AAA innings translate to a 9.4 K/9 in MLB context, respectable company, but the walk rate buries everything underneath it. At AAA he's posting 9.2 BB/9, and translated to the big-league level that comes out to 7.3, more than double what a typical MLB starter allows; the K-BB% sits at just 5 percent at AAA, and the MLB equivalent lands at 7.4 where the league norm is 13.5. Eighty-seven walks in 85 innings is a pitcher who is actively battling himself more than hitters. If the control ever firms up, the strikeout rate is a real foundation to build on, but right now the only realistic outcome is a depth arm, and that ceiling only gets reached if the walk rate falls enough to make the strikeouts matter.

reports.name: Willi Castro
reports.published_report: The .310 xwOBA tells you most of what you need to know: Castro makes contact that plays below average and chases pitches at a 38.1% clip, which is why the expected batting average sits at .233 despite the projection carrying a .261 AVG. The power is shaped more by barrel rate, where his 8.6% is near the middle of the league, than by exit velocity, which at 87.6 mph runs well below average. What saves the profile is 28.2 ft/s sprint speed and genuine positional flexibility, enough to keep a low-end regular's stat line, around .752 OPS over 540 plate appearances in the projection, plausible if Colorado's park does its usual work on that batted ball mix. If the chase rate doesn't come down and the home environment stops carrying the AVG, you're looking at a useful bench piece who can play four spots rather than an everyday player who earns his lineup spot on merit.

reports.name: Cal Raleigh

A 12.8% barrel rate sits in the same card as a 31.6% whiff rate and a 36.3% chase rate, which means he squares up when he connects, and he connects less and less often. The xBA of .180 is essentially a 1st-percentile outcome, and when you pair that with a 32.3% strikeout rate, the .294 xwOBA stops looking like a floor and starts looking like a ceiling that requires contact luck to reach. ValuCast's projection of .175/.282/.340 across 516 PA isn't pessimism; it's arithmetic from a contact profile that's broken, sitting on top of legitimate thump that can't carry an average into usable territory — and if the chase rate doesn't move, the projected 20 home runs won't be enough to keep him in the everyday conversation.

Across AA & A+, Junior Sanchez carries a 10.3 K/9 and a 3.2 BB/9, the kind of ratio that produces a 20 K-BB% on the minor-league side, but the MLB-equivalent read softens it: the strikeout rate comes back to 8.2 per nine, a tick below a league-average 8.6, and the walk rate edges slightly above average at 3.5. The peripherals at 20 years old in Double-A are genuinely encouraging, especially that 1.2 WHIP and 3.7 ERA across 93 innings, and the zone control has real teeth in the minors. If the strikeout stuff doesn't carry the translation, what's left is a back-end arm who commands the zone well enough to survive, a depth piece rather than a rotation fixture.

reports.name: Nate Furman
reports.published_report: The contact is the whole argument. Furman is hitting .284 at AAA with a 12% strikeout rate across 434 plate appearances — that translates to a 16.1% K% at the MLB level, well below what the average big-leaguer runs at 22.0%, which is the clearest tool he's carrying. The ISO at .122 in AAA translates to .114, and seven home runs in 434 trips confirms there's no sneaky pop hiding in the profile. If the bat-to-ball skill holds and he gets on base at the clip his .370 OBP and 48 walks suggest he can, the floor is a useful bench piece; if a major-league staff decides to challenge him and the contact rate slips, there's nothing else in the profile to carry the day.

reports.name: Wilder Dalis
reports.published_report: The surface numbers are loud: .307/.402/.574 across A+ & A, with 16 home runs and 24 stolen bags in 318 plate appearances, and his OPS and SLG percentiles sit at 98 against the hitter pool. The ISO translates to .157 in MLB equivalent terms, close to the MLB average of .150, which tells you the raw pop earns its keep in context but won't overwhelm better pitching. His K% at 24 across A+ & A translates to 28% against MLB pitching, notably higher than the MLB average of 22%, and that's the hinge: if the swing decisions generating 41 walks don't hold as the stuff gets better, the offensive profile degrades toward a bench outcome quickly. At 19, with that combination of contact rate, power output, and speed, this is either a developing everyday third baseman or, if the strikeout rate eats him alive at higher levels, a depth piece who aged out of his tools.

reports.name: Michael Lombardi
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is doing a lot of heavy lifting here, and the walk rate is threatening to drop it. Lombardi is punching out batters at 12.8 per nine across 80.3 innings at A-ball, a clip that translates to 8.5 per nine at the MLB level, nearly indistinguishable from what an average big-league starter produces. The problem is the 5.4 walks per nine translates to 5.5, while MLB starters average 3.2, and that gap is what caps the ceiling at a depth arm. If the control tightens as he climbs, there's a functional pitcher here; if it doesn't, the strikeouts stop covering the walks and the floor is the ceiling too.

reports.name: Peter Lambert
reports.published_report: The xERA of 3.44 is the number that tells you what he actually is, and it sits comfortably ahead of his walk rate. That 9.3 BB% is the profile's load-bearing flaw — the strikeout rate at 23.5% won't overpower mistakes, and a 93.9 mph fastball leaves him without a velocity margin for error when the command wavers. What works is contact suppression: a 6.8 barrel rate and 37.2 hard-hit rate that both shade toward average, meaning he's keeping barrels down rather than blowing hitters away, and the xwOBA of .288 shows that's translating into real quality-of-contact control. If the walk rate firms up even modestly, the projected 3.49 ERA and 153.9 innings look like a genuine mid-rotation season; if it doesn't, he's a back-end starter who needs everything else to go right.

reports.name: Dylan O'Rae
reports.published_report: The .406 OBP at AA is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's sitting on top of a 16% walk rate and just 63 strikeouts across 359 plate appearances. Dylan O'Rae doesn't hit for power, full stop: his .097 ISO at AA translates to a .101 MLB equivalent, well short of the .150 MLB average, and 2 home runs in 359 trips confirms this isn't a gap in the data. What he actually is: a left-handed second baseman who gets on base at a genuine clip, runs (48 stolen bases at AA this season), and puts the ball in play without striking out, with a walk rate that would clear the 8.5% MLB average by a comfortable margin. If the on-base skill holds as the pitching sharpens, he's a useful piece in a lineup; if the .348 BABIP backing that average regresses and the power never emerges, he's a bench bat who draws walks.

reports.name: Corey Seager
reports.published_report: The 15.1% barrel rate is the spine of this profile, and everything else hangs off the tension between it and a 34.0% whiff rate. When Seager makes contact, he's doing genuine damage, a .456 xSLG and 91.3 mph average exit velocity say the pop is consistent, not streaky, but he's making contact less often than almost anyone with his power profile, which is what drives the projection's .221 AVG down well below what his .231 xBA already implies. The 12.0% walk rate keeps his projected .317 OBP from cratering, so the real question isn't the power, it's whether 419 projected plate appearances reflects health holding or slipping. If he stays on the field and the barrel rate sustains, the 19 projected home runs in that PA total are underselling what the contact quality earns; if the whiff rate climbs further, the average erodes and so does the lineup value.

reports.name: Brandon Nimmo
reports.published_report: The xBA of .291 with a 96th-percentile mark tells you the contact quality is legitimately elite, and the 51.2% hard-hit rate backs it up — this is a hitter who punishes the ball when he gets to it. What's keeping the projection modest is the walk rate: 8.2% is below the league median for a hitter with this kind of bat-to-ball profile, and without the on-base padding, .340 OBP is the ceiling rather than the floor. The Statcast contact grades point to something closer to his .497 xSLG than his projected .438 SLG, so the power upside has both the exit velocity and the hard-hit rate behind it, and 18 home runs across 655 PA feels conservative if the underlying contact holds. He's a solid everyday outfielder for Texas, and the gap between what the ball-tracking data says and what the counting stats will show is almost entirely a walk-rate story.

reports.name: Willy Adames
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is nearly all bad news. His xBA sits at .217 and his xwOBA at .289, both bottom-decile marks, built on an 87.2 mph average exit velocity and a 28.7% whiff rate that together explain why the contact rarely does damage. The 8.3% barrel rate is the one counterpoint, right at league average, and that's where the 25 projected home runs come from, a power output that looks disconnected from everything else in the profile but isn't impossible if he keeps lifting the ball when he does make contact. At a .225/.291/.410 projection across 649 plate appearances, he's a shortstop who earns his roster spot almost entirely through position scarcity and pop, and if the strikeout rate climbs further from its already-heavy 27.4%, what's left is a bottom-of-the-order bat that costs you more than it gives.

Luke Stevenson's 22% walk rate at the level translates to 14.6% against an MLB average of 8.5%, which means the discipline isn't a mirage of the level, it survives the conversion. The ISO translates to .159, right at league average, so the 16 home runs at A+ suggest enough raw pop to at least hold that line, though 109 strikeouts alongside those walks means the contact profile is genuinely thin. The whole thing hinges on whether the bat-to-ball ever tightens behind a catcher's frame, because if the strikeout rate stays at 30.7% equivalent in a major league park, the walk-and-power game gives you an interesting bench piece at best, and the floor here is exactly that.

reports.name: Isaac Lyon
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the whole argument here. The problem is the strikeout side: 86 punchouts across those same 95 innings translates to a 7.2 K/9 MLB-equivalent, well short of what the average MLB arm produces, which means the profile only works if the control holds and everything gets put in play softly. reports.name: Kyle Leahy
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile is the problem. A 5.08 xERA and a 47.7% hard-hit rate, second percentile among pitchers, tells you what hitters are doing when they make contact, and the 26.7% chase rate confirms they're getting plenty of chances to do it. Leahy throws enough strikes, a 7.0% walk rate is genuinely useful, but he can't miss bats at 21.1% K% and can't limit damage when they swing. The projection's 3.58 ERA over 158.7 innings requires a level of strand-rate and sequencing luck that the underlying contact quality makes hard to sustain. If the soft-contact shape never develops, what's left is a strike-thrower who eats innings until lineups figure out they don't need to chase.

reports.name: Yolfran Castillo
reports.published_report: The bat-to-ball skills and the legs are loud; the power is the question. Yolfran Castillo is posting a 14% strikeout rate across A+ & A at 19 years old, translating to roughly 19.9% at the MLB level, well below what the average big-league hitter runs up, and he's drawn 63 walks to build a .383 OBP in 479 plate appearances. He's also stolen 48 bases. The ISO across A+ & A sits at .119, and the MLB-equivalent reads .095 while the typical MLB hitter sits at .150 — that gap is the whole argument, because a profile this contact-heavy and speed-reliant needs at least fringe power to profile as something more than a utility piece. If the power never develops, he's a bench bat who gets on base and runs; if it does, the contact rate and walk rate together are a legitimate foundation for a regular shortstop.

reports.name: Sean Keys
reports.published_report: The power is loud enough to make you stop scrolling: .290 ISO across AAA & AA, a .567 SLG, 23 home runs in 368 plate appearances. Translated to an MLB context, that raw thump comes out to a .199 ISO against a league that typically sits around .150, which is a real gap. The walk rate translates similarly well, 11.4% against an 8.5% baseline, so the .408 OBP isn't just a product of him running into pitches. The whole thing hinges on one uncomfortable fact: he's a 23-year-old first baseman, and a first baseman who doesn't hit at the absolute top of the position doesn't have a fallback skill to hide behind — if the strikeouts tick up at the big-league level (his translated K% is already a tick above league average), the defensive profile offers no cushion, and you're looking at a bench bat who only plays against lefties when the roster needs a body.

reports.name: Hector Osorio
reports.published_report: The discipline numbers are the loudest thing in this profile. Across A+ & A, Hector Osorio has walked 54 times against just 50 strikeouts in 394 plate appearances, a combination that translates to an 18.4% strikeout rate at the MLB level, well below what most big-league hitters produce. The .295/.411/.543 line is backed by a .291 BABIP, so there's no luck tax coming due, and the .248 ISO across A+ & A translates to .154 at the MLB level, right at what the average big leaguer produces. If the plate discipline holds as competition stiffens, he becomes an everyday center fielder; if the contact rate quietly erodes against better secondaries, what's left is a bench bat who walks enough to stay on a roster but doesn't punish mistakes consistently enough to start.

reports.name: Jack Hurley
reports.published_report: The translation is the problem. Across AAA & AA in 204 plate appearances, Hurley is hitting .254/.332/.409, which looks passable until you run it through the MLB equivalent and find a strikeout rate of 25.5% where the league sits at 22.0, paired with a translated ISO of .135 where the league average lands at .150. The contact-and-power combo that would need to work together doesn't clear the bar at either end. If the hit tool sharpens and the strikeout rate drops, there's a low-end regular hiding in a left field profile; if it doesn't, 15 walks in 204 plate appearances across AAA & AA is the whole argument, and that's a bench bat at best.

reports.name: Marvin Alcantara
reports.published_report: The stolen bases are doing heavy lifting here. Fifteen at AA in 306 plate appearances is genuine production, but the rest of the offensive profile is thin enough that it can't carry the profile alone. His MLB-equivalent translation puts ISO at .119 where the average sits at .150, and his walk rate translates to 6.8% where the average sits at 8.5%, meaning the .238/.288/.368 AA line reflects a hitter who misses bats at a manageable rate but without the on-base skills or power to profile as more than a fringe regular. If the legs translate and the walk rate creeps up, he's a useful bench piece who gives a roster a specific skill; if neither develops, this is organizational depth at second base.

reports.name: Jadher Areinamo
reports.published_report: The power profile at AA is the most interesting thing here, and also the thing that shrinks the most on translation. A .189 ISO across 293 PA at AA reads well on the card, but the MLB-equivalent drops to .146, roughly what a league-average bat produces, and the walk rate translates to 6.6% against a baseline that most big-league regulars clear comfortably. The contact side is quieter than the raw line suggests: a .277 BABIP holding up a .256 average, with 57 strikeouts kept manageable but an OBP of .302 that leaves almost no margin. If the power stays near that translated floor and the walk rate doesn't grow, what's left is a middle-infield profile that fits a bench role more than a lineup spot.

reports.name: Jesus Rodriguez
reports.published_report: The strikeout rate is the whole argument. At AAA in 2026, Jesus Rodriguez has fanned just 25 times across 221 plate appearances, an 11% clip that translates to a 16.9% MLB-equivalent rate against a league where most hitters whiff closer to 22.0%. He has drawn 24 walks against those same 25 strikeouts, and that contact-and-patience combination at catcher is what the profile lives on, because the power is not going to carry anyone: the .131 ISO at AAA translates to .126 MLB-equivalent, light for the position. If the contact rate holds, he becomes a bench or platoon catcher with a real reason to be on a roster; if major-league velocity flattens it, what remains is a depth receiver without enough bat to matter.

reports.name: Ben Kudrna
reports.published_report:
Two innings. That's the entire current AAA sample, and it's doing almost no work here.

What the translation shows isn't alarming but isn't encouraging: a K/9 that matches the MLB average exactly at 8.6, a BB/9 of 3.8 where the average sits at 3.2, and a K-BB% of 12.4 when the typical MLB starter lands at 13.5. If the strikeout rate doesn't climb and the walks stay where they are, the profile resolves as a depth arm, which is exactly where the ceiling lands anyway. The honest read here is that 2.0 IP can't tell you much, and ValuCast's rankings reflect that uncertainty, sliding him six spots in three days.
